statedVsRealGaps: Title 'Data Analyst/Manager' and roleFamily 'data_ai' frame an analytics seat, but the JD is dominated by operational management: billing/revenue-cycle compliance, line-supervision of a team, and inter-agency HIT relationship management. Analysis is one of several streams, not the center of gravity.
Stated stack is empty; the real toolset is heavily domain-specific health-IT (PSYCKES, lead-HH EHRs, Medicaid claims/remittance, HHDB, NADAP systems) — none surfaced in the structured need.

seniorityTarget is 'senior', yet the formal floor is only a Bachelor's degree with a blank years-of-experience field, and the role is characterized as 'frequent but relatively minor' change — the credential bar undersells the breadth and accountability actually described.
JD calls for 'statistical reporting metrics and methods' but names no analytics tooling (SQL, BI, statistical software); the technical analytics competency is implied rather than specified.
Billing compliance is explicitly the primary responsibility and is financially/regulatorily material, but the analyst-flavored title risks attracting candidates who treat it as secondary.
riskAreas: Role conflation — one seat fuses senior analytics, Medicaid billing/revenue-cycle compliance, health-IT integration, and people management; a single hire strong in one dimension is likely weak in another, and screening can easily optimize for the wrong one.

Heavy NY Medicaid Health Home domain dependency (PSYCKES, claims/MAPP-style billing, lead-HH dynamics) means a generic data analyst faces a steep ramp; transferable analytics skill alone is insufficient.
Financial/audit exposure — owning billing QA and reimbursement integrity makes errors directly costly and audit-visible.
PHI/HIPAA exposure — working across EHRs and PSYCKES requires data-governance and privacy discipline not mentioned in the JD.
Matrixed accountability — depends on external partner HIT teams and the NADAP database team for outcomes the role is accountable for, i.e. responsibility without full control.
Vague experience floor weakens screening; the formal minimums won't gate candidates for the real scope, raising mis-hire risk.
analysis.reflection: This is a grounded, extractable non-software role, so the absence of a codebase is expected — the real 'body of work' is a Medicaid Health Home data ecosystem (PSYCKES, lead-Health-Home EHRs, the HHDB, claims/remittance billing, and NADAP-shared systems). Reflected against that evidence, the structured need understates the job. It is filed as 'Data Analyst/Manager' / data_ai, but the JD's own weighting puts billing-compliance ownership first, followed by team supervision (including hiring and discipline) and inter-agency HIT relationship management; outcomes analytics is genuinely senior but is one stream among several. The biggest divergences are (1) an empty stated stack versus a substantial, domain-locked health-IT toolset, and (2) a 'senior' target paired with a soft formal floor (Bachelor's, blank years, 'minor' change) that doesn't match the real accountability for reimbursement, PHI, and a direct-report team. True complexity is high because of the breadth-plus-domain combination, and the chief hiring risk is role conflation: pick a candidate who is genuinely tri-lingual across analytics, Medicaid billing compliance, and people leadership, or expect a gap on whichever leg is under-screened.

case.title: Health Home Data: Billing Integrity & Outcomes You Can Defend
case.brief: You are stepping into the senior Data Analyst/Manager seat for a NADAP-style lead Health Home operation. We handed you a small, de-identified synthetic data drop (no real PHI) that mirrors what actually lands on this desk: a MAPP-HHTS-style claims/remittance extract, the internal HHDB enrollment roster, a PSYCKES inpatient export, HH-EHR encounter rows, a stale member crosswalk, an incomplete data dictionary, the prior analyst's legacy billing-QA checklist, and a one-paragraph ask from senior management. Your job is not to type SQL fast — assume any query, script, or spreadsheet formula can be generated for you. Your job is to make defensible calls about messy, matrixed, audit-visible health data: where billable activity leaked, what the program's outcomes really are, and what you would tell leadership. Several of the materials disagree with each other or with the dictionary on purpose; that is the realistic part. Budget ~2 hours and stop at the cap — depth on a few decisions beats breadth. Throughout, keep a short DECISIONS log (normal practice here): for every place the materials were ambiguous or contradictory, jot what you chose, the alternative you rejected, and the one question you'd put to the central database team, a lead-HH HIT partner, or management. Deliverables can be a notebook, spreadsheet, and/or short memo — whatever lets a reviewer follow your reasoning. State assumptions explicitly; we care more about how you reasoned to a number than about the number itself.
case.repoSeed:
A de-identified, synthetic Health Home data drop (no real PHI; values are fabricated but the shapes, quirks, and contradictions are realistic). Files handed to the candidate:

1) claims_remittance_2025Q3.csv — MAPP-HHTS-style billing extract, one row per member-segment-month. Columns: hhdb_member_id, segment_month, rate_code, billing_status {draft|submitted|accepted|rejected}, submitted_date, remittance_status {pending|paid|denied|void}, paid_amount, denial_reason. Note: billing_status and remittance_status are independent stages; some 'submitted' rows never reach 'paid', and a handful of duplicate segment-months exist for the same member.

2) hh_enrollment_HHDB.csv — internal HHDB roster. Columns: hhdb_member_id, cin, enroll_date, disenroll_date, reenroll_flag, lead_hh, care_manager, acuity_tier. Some members have two non-contiguous enrollment spans (re-enrollment).

3) psyckes_inpatient_export.csv — NYS OMH PSYCKES inpatient/quality export keyed on cin. Columns: cin, admit_date, discharge_date, readmit_30d_flag, data_through_date. A header note states PSYCKES claims-based data runs ~3-6 months behind, so the most recent months are incomplete.

4) hh_ehr_encounters.csv — lead-HH EHR care-management contacts. Columns: ehr_member_id, service_date, contact_type, minutes. Keyed on ehr_member_id, NOT on cin or hhdb_member_id.

5) member_id_crosswalk.xlsx — a hand-maintained, stale crosswalk: hhdb_member_id <-> cin <-> ehr_member_id, last refreshed before the latest re-enrollments. Contains blanks, a few one-to-many rows, and at least one cin mapped to two ehr_member_ids.

6) data_dictionary.md — partial and inconsistent. It defines most fields but is silent or contradictory on the semantics of enroll_date (referral date vs. activation/consent date) and on whether segment_month counts the calendar month of service or of submission.

7) billing_qa_checklist_legacy.xlsx — the prior analyst's QA checks (e.g., 'sum of submitted = expected'), which look reasonable but miss the dominant failure mode.

8) mgmt_request_memo.md — one paragraph from senior management: 'Board meeting Thursday — show me billing is healthy and that the Health Home is keeping people out of the hospital. One number each is fine.'
tasks: Build the member spine. Using member_id_crosswalk.xlsx, hh_enrollment_HHDB.csv, and data_dictionary.md, construct the member-level join across HHDB (hhdb_member_id), PSYCKES (cin), and HH-EHR (ehr_member_id) that the other tasks depend on. Report join coverage explicitly — matched, unmatched, and duplicated members — decide and document how you treat re-enrollment spans and the stale/one-to-many crosswalk rows, and state the PHI/HIPAA handling you would apply to this linked dataset. Do not assume the obvious key joins cleanly.

Reconcile billing integrity. From claims_remittance_2025Q3.csv against the HHDB enrollment spans, quantify (a) billable Health Home member-months that were never submitted (revenue leakage) and (b) member-months submitted but not reimbursed (rejected/denied/pending), keeping billing_status and remittance_status as distinct stages and handling duplicate segment rows. Identify the single largest systemic root cause and specify one concrete QA control that would have caught it. Assess whether billing_qa_checklist_legacy.xlsx would have caught it — and if not, say why.

Define an outcomes metric you can defend. Using psyckes_inpatient_export.csv and the enrollment spans, compute a pre-vs-post-enrollment inpatient hospitalization rate (and a 30-day readmission rate) for the cohort. Hand back BOTH the number and the exact metric definition: state your index date, the pre and post observation windows, the denominator, and how you handle PSYCKES reporting lag, unequal member tenure, and re-enrollment. Note any bias that could make a naive before/after comparison overstate the program's effect.

Brief senior management and log your decisions. Write a one-page memo answering the mgmt_request_memo.md ask — but first pin down what 'billing is healthy' and 'keeping people out of the hospital' should actually mean before reporting a single number, and name what you would need from the NADAP central database team or lead-HH HIT partners to stand behind it. Attach your DECISIONS log: for each ambiguous or contradictory point you hit across the materials, record what you chose, the alternative you rejected, and the question you'd ask the team.

coverProbes.where: Task 2 — claims_remittance_2025Q3.csv, where billing_status (draft/submitted/accepted/rejected) and remittance_status (pending/paid/denied/void) are separate stages and duplicate segment-months exist.
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate treats 'submitted' as an intent, not revenue — reconciling to remittance_status and paid_amount, de-duplicating segments, and reporting leakage at the right stage. A naive one-shot sums submitted rows (or matches the legacy checklist's 'sum of submitted = expected'), reports a healthy-looking total, passes a shallow row-count/sum check, and silently misses denials, never-paid claims, and double-counted duplicates.
decisionSpace: Measure leakage as eligible-but-unsubmitted member-months (submission completeness) — surfaces process gaps but ignores denied dollars.
Measure leakage as submitted-but-unreimbursed dollars (denials + aging pending) — surfaces revenue at risk but assumes submission was complete.
Net reimbursement per eligible member-month end-to-end — most complete and audit-defensible but needs the most assumptions about eligibility and rate codes.

coverProbes.where: Task 3 — psyckes_inpatient_export.csv (data_through_date lag note) combined with variable enrollment tenure and re-enrollment spans.
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate normalizes to per-member-month over equal pre/post windows, drops the lag-incomplete recent tail, and explicitly names regression-to-the-mean / immortal-time bias (people enroll right after a crisis admission). A naive candidate counts crude admissions before vs. after across unequal windows and reports a large, flattering 'reduction' that is an artifact of the lag and the enrollment trigger, not the program.
decisionSpace: Per-member-month rate over fixed equal pre/post windows, excluding lag-incomplete months — comparable and bias-aware, but discards recent data and shrinks the cohort.
Crude before/after admission counts with caveats stated — fast and intuitive but vulnerable to unequal tenure and regression to the mean.
Time-to-event / survival framing on the post period — most rigorous on censoring and lag, but heavier and harder to put on a board slide.

coverProbes.where: Task 1 — member_id_crosswalk.xlsx (stale, one-to-many, blanks) plus data_dictionary.md's silence/contradiction on enroll_date (referral vs. activation) and segment_month (service vs. submission month).
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate reads the dictionary and crosswalk first, discovers cin↔ehr_member_id is not 1:1 and the crosswalk predates recent re-enrollments, reports unmatched/duplicated coverage, and consciously picks an enroll_date definition because it sets both billing eligibility and the pre/post index date. A naive candidate joins on the first plausible key, silently drops unmatched members and double-counts duplicates, and never notices the index-date choice that quietly drives every downstream number.
decisionSpace: Drop unmatched/ambiguous members and report on the clean subset — defensible and conservative, but biases the cohort and understates leakage.
Collapse one-to-many crosswalk rows to a best-match per member and flag confidence — keeps coverage high at the cost of some wrong links.

Keep all rows, mark match-quality and date-semantics assumptions, and reconcile with the central database team — most transparent but leaves open items the candidate must escalate rather than resolve alone.

coverProbes.where: Task 4 — mgmt_request_memo.md ('show me billing is healthy and that we're keeping people out of the hospital — one number each is fine').
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate refuses to ship a vanity number blind: they define what 'healthy' and 'impact' should mean for a board/funder audience, state the trade-offs of each candidate metric, and name what they'd confirm with the central database team or lead-HH HIT partners before standing behind it. A naive candidate answers the literal request with a single unqualified figure and inherits whatever bias the data carried.
decisionSpace: Report submission/collection completeness and clean-claim rate — operationally honest and audit-aligned, but less of a headline.
Report net reimbursement vs. expected and days-in-AR — the CFO/audit view, but needs eligibility and rate assumptions made explicit.
Report dollars reimbursed plus the caveated outcomes delta as a paired story — most useful to a board, but requires saying clearly what is not yet defensible.
